issues.title: Use "site", not Origin
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
Privacy Pass made a serious error in using "origin" to describe the thing the tokens grant access to.  In practice, the privacy unit on the web is a [site](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#site).  That is, the set of web origins that share a registrable domain.

Because the website is something of a bystander in MoLE processing[^1], it's not a load-bearing notion, but I think that using "site" as the name of the primary beneficiary of the protocol is right.

[^1]: In practice the moderator is the one involved in the protocol interactions on behalf of each site.  The site really only has a few interactions: first, to identify a moderator; second, to receive the moderator's verdict about the client; and, third, to provide the moderator with feedback about interactions with the client.

issues.author: wbl
issues.body: In MOLE we want abstractly clients to update their endorsements. However, the way we implement this is by having them reveal identifiers for an issued thing, and then getting back another issued thing. Right now our terminology mixes these levels, using credential for both. I'd like to differentiate between the cryptographic artifact and the state that is being managed

comments.body:
The way I see this is endorsement is what you get from the anchor. It is NOT updated by the moderator.

Moderator are delivering credentials, which MAY (SHOULD?) be updated.

This is discussed in the [terminology section](https://moderation-of-unlinkable-endorsements.github.io/internet-drafts/draft-schlesinger-mole-architecture.html#name-conventions-and-definitions). comments.author: wbl
comments.body:
Somehow I missed that section but there's still a conceptual distinction to be made:
A credential update works by the client burning something it has, and getting something back from the moderator. That thing needs a name, but it isn't the credential (which we conceptualize as always existing), and i think it would be clearer if we spelled it out.

Alternatively I don't see why we need to have two separate names for the anchor to moderator and moderator to moderator flows. Yes they are very different, but they are both functionally similar. Calling them credentials, and the information that is transmitted an endorsement might work (but it's pretty different information, maybe just making them credentials work).

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
Following discussion, my impression is that having distinctive name for _anchor material_ and _moderator material_ is good. In my view, _endorsement_ works for anchor material, but credential is a bit broad for moderator material.

From @etrouton (if I'm understanding correctly), having something that reflect accumulation over time would be best. Personal suggestions would be _accumulator_ or _momentum_, with a preference for _accumulator_.

This would allow the use of "credential" for all steps as an underlying realisation, with a disambiguation about the state.

issues.title: Should moderator identity be included in the nullifier
issues.author: ekr
issues.body: I've been reviewing the Longfellow mechanism (Section 4.2 of -protocol) and it seems like the nullifier just includes the epoch. As I've discussed with a few of you for Webbotauth, I think it's going to be desirable to sometimes use the same Endorsement with multiple Moderators, because we're leaning less on scarcity and more on the validation of the client. If I'm reading the description correctly, this will currently result in linkability. I think this can be readily addressed by including the identity of the Moderator in the computation of the nullifier, along with the epoch. Presumably we could have both Endorsements that allow this and forbid it, as desired.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
I think this is right for Longfellow.
Longfellow in [section 4.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-jms-mole-protocols-00#name-longfellow) gives you a per epoch and global nullifier. I agree that we could derive a nullifier per moderator. This is probably desireable to support late binding of the endorsement to specific moderators.

However, that does not apply directly to IHAT, which requires the nullifier to be known at the time of endorsement. This implies that it cannot rely on the client knowing the moderator "identity" which is only known at the "Redeem & Issue" phase, possibly further down the line.

So to your suggestion
1. Longfellow could work in both modes,
2. IHAT would be restricted to a global nullifier and one-time use. Issuance and verification are orders of magnitude faster and smaller than with Longfellow, at the cost of more RTT and no late binding.

For IHAT, i'd double check with someone closer to the crypto work.

comments.author: wbl
comments.body: IHAT is fundamentally a one time token, and complicated by its support for issuer-hiding, which I don't think WebBotAuth needs. The tradeoffs with MOLE are a bit different, even if both could use similar looking ideas.

pulls.author: thibmeu
pulls.body:
This PR aggregates MoLE drafts (architecture, crypto, and HTTP transport) into one repository as discussed in #2.

It also updates the architecture draft to use "Site" terminology, adds co-authors, and describes the three main flows: Endorsement, Credential Issuance, and Credential Presentation/Updates. It also adds early placeholder drafts for protocol token types (as a placeholder crypto API for issuer-hiding) and HTTP transport (placeholder as well).

This is intended to make the document structure and open design questions easier to review and to work on.

pulls.title: protocols: specify the endorsement and credential protocols
pulls.author: thibmeu
pulls.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This change is rather large, because the drafts were mostly empty. I think having a high level about the compositions, then individual protocols (endorsement/credential) would be useful. If that helps, happy to push this commit as its own branch on the main github repository, so that it is rendered by github actions. The PR is meant to provide a more concrete set of discussion, and text mentions that the set of protocols is subject to change at the time of writting.

Start specifying protocols to give a more concrete hook of MoLE.

This commit adds:
1. One section per protocol with its type value, configuration, messages, and behavior,
2. Two endorsement protocols (IHAT, a placeholder name pending the crypto draft, and Longfellow over legacy credentials),
3. Three credential protocols (ACT, Privacy Pass with a reverse flow, budget Privacy Pass construction).

Design decisions worth knowing about:

- Generic envelopes, per-type structures. Every endorsement type defines `Challenge` and `Presentation`. Every credential type defines `Challenge`, `IssuanceRequest`, `IssuanceResponse`, `PresentationAndUpdate`, and `Update`. The http-transport have been updated accordingly (as that draft defined these names initially).
- Redeem & Issue is an authorization, so it uses the Mole auth scheme like presentation does. `Mole-Credential` is the single response header: `response=` for issuance, `update=` after a presentation. Is this the right move: TBD,
- Anchor interactions are left to the protocols draft, which uses POST,
- Challenge binding is clarified. It hashes the decoded challenge octets, and not the base64url ASCII header,
- Clients grease with reserved `0x?A?A` credential types so Moderators keep handling unknown types and absent presentations,
- Two registries: one for endorsement, one for credentials,
- Remove `Site` from the HTTP transport draft.

Key rotation and discovery, privacy considerations, and security considerations are mostly left as TODO.

There is a full example in the appendix.

The crypto bits that were in the previous protocol draft have been split to a `-crypto` draft.

Note: I still have not added authors beyond myself to the `http-transport` and `-protocols` draft, mostly to request consent. @dennisjackson @SamuelSchlesinger you can just say yes and we'll do that before any publication
